text: {"master_id": "matt-warnock", "work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "usage_notes": [{"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-chord-voicing-introduction", "narrative": "Warnock prescribes Dm7 as the ii chord entry point for all jazz guitar study, introduced as one of four core chord shapes to be memorized over the ii V I progression. Students learn the voicing in isolation first, then with metronome, then over backing track: 'Start by playing these chords on your own, memorize them, and then add in a metronome when ready.' Chapter 1 (book chapter), p. 4.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 2 (book ch. 1) p. 4"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-chord-freddie-green-rhythmic-placement", "narrative": "For min7 in the ii function, Warnock prescribes the Freddie Green rhythm as the first comping approach: one chord per beat in quarter notes, with accents on beats 2 and 4. 'The rhythm is all quarter notes, meaning you play one chord per beat... accent the 2nd and 4th chords/beats in each bar. This imitates the hi-hat and helps you bring a higher level of swing to the rhythm.' Chapter 1, p. 5.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 2 (book ch. 1) p. 5"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-chord-charleston-rhythmic-placement", "narrative": "After the Freddie Green rhythm is internalized on Dm7, Warnock prescribes adding the Charleston rhythm -- chord on beat 1 and the & of 2 -- before mixing both patterns freely. 'This rhythm places the first chord on beat 1 of each bar, then the second chord is on the & of 2, between beats 2 and 3 in each bar.' Chapter 1, p. 6.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 2 (book ch. 1) p. 6"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-chord-approach-chord-chromatic-displacement", "narrative": "For min7 as the ii chord, Warnock prescribes chromatic approach chords: take the Dm7 voicing shape and play it one fret above (approach from above) or one fret below (approach from below), then resolve into the target chord. 'Approach chords are where you play a chromatic chord one fret above or below the target chord you're aiming for.' The approach-from-above direction is practiced before below, then both are mixed. Chapter 3, p. 11-12.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 4 (book ch. 3) p. 11-12"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "min7", "function_role": "ii-chord-bass-first-picking-pattern", "narrative": "Warnock prescribes a bass-first picking pattern for Dm7 (and the full ii V I) when playing solo or without a bassist: separate the bass note from the melody in the picking hand. 'The first picking exercise separates the bass from the melody. This type of comping pattern is helpful when there's no bassist in your group, when you play solo guitar, or for technical development.' Learn bass-first before melody-first. Chapter 2, p. 9.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 3 (book ch. 2) p. 9"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "v-chord-voicing-introduction", "narrative": "G7 is introduced as the V chord of the core ii V I vocabulary alongside Dm7 and Cmaj7/Cmaj9. Warnock prescribes learning it as part of the four-chord block -- 'here are four chords that fit over the ii V I progression' -- in the sequence: solo practice, metronome, backing track, rhythmic variation. Chapter 1, p. 4.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 2 (book ch. 1) p. 4"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "v-chord-freddie-green-rhythmic-placement", "narrative": "For G7 in the V function, Warnock prescribes the same Freddie Green quarter-note comping as the first rhythmic approach: one chord per beat with 2-and-4 accents for swing feel. This is the first named rhythm applied systematically to all chords in the progression before introducing the Charleston or approach-chord techniques. Chapter 1, p. 5.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 2 (book ch. 1) p. 5"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "v-chord-approach-chord-chromatic-displacement", "narrative": "For G7 as the V chord, Warnock prescribes the same chromatic approach-chord treatment as all chords in the progression: move the voicing shape one fret above or below and resolve into the target. 'Approach chords bring a tension and release sound to your comping, jazzing up your chords along the way.' The dominant function makes this tension-release especially apt. Chapter 3, p. 11.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 4 (book ch. 3) p. 11"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "v-chord-scale-choice-for-soloing", "narrative": "For soloing over G7 as the V chord of a ii V I, Warnock prescribes using the tonic major scale (C major) rather than a separate dominant scale. 'Because all 3 chords in a ii V I are in the parent key, so Dm7-G7-Cmaj7 are all in C major, you can use the tonic major scale to solo over all of those chords.' No chord-specific scale substitution is taught for dom7 in this method. Chapter 4, p. 14.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:major-scale-fretboard-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 5 (book ch. 4) p. 14"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "i-chord-voicing-lead-sheet-color-expansion", "narrative": "For Cmaj7 as the I chord, Warnock prescribes reading the lead-sheet symbol but voicing the richer Cmaj9 color: 'In jazz, you normally see the simplest chord symbol written on a lead sheet, then you as the performer color that chord from there. So, it's good to get used to seeing Cmaj7 but playing the Cmaj9 color as it imitates a real-life musical situation.' Chapter 3, p. 11.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 4 (book ch. 3) p. 11"}], "provenance": "extracted", "cross_ref": ["maj7/i-chord-bare-voicing-in-performance"]}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "i-chord-bare-voicing-in-performance", "narrative": "Warnock implicitly proscribes playing the bare Cmaj7 voicing in performance contexts where the lead sheet shows Cmaj7: the convention in jazz is that the written symbol is the minimum, not the target. Playing Cmaj7 without added color (e.g., the 9th) fails to meet real-world performance expectation. 'It's good to get used to seeing Cmaj7 but playing the Cmaj9 color as it imitates a real-life musical situation.' Chapter 3, p. 11.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 4 (book ch. 3) p. 11"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive", "cross_ref": ["maj7/i-chord-voicing-lead-sheet-color-expansion"]}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "i-chord-freddie-green-rhythmic-placement", "narrative": "For Cmaj7/Cmaj9 as the I chord, Warnock prescribes the Freddie Green quarter-note comping as the foundational rhythmic approach -- all four beats, accents on 2 and 4 -- before introducing syncopated or approach-chord treatments. This establishes the harmonic landing point of the progression with maximum metric support. Chapter 1, p. 5.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 2 (book ch. 1) p. 5"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "i-chord-approach-chord-chromatic-displacement", "narrative": "For Cmaj7 (voiced as Cmaj9) as the I chord, Warnock prescribes approach chords as a comping color device: 'The first exercise features approach chords from above, where you play the same shape one fret higher, then resolve into your target chord from there.' The identical mechanic applies from below. Resolution into the maj7 target is mandatory -- the approach is incomplete without it. Chapter 3, p. 12.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 4 (book ch. 3) p. 12"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "i-chord-melody-first-picking-pattern", "narrative": "For Cmaj7 and the I chord in chord-melody or chord-soloing contexts, Warnock prescribes the melody-first picking pattern to highlight the top voice: 'Bringing out the melody is useful for comping, chord soloing, and especially chord melody playing.' Learn this after the bass-first pattern. Chapter 2, p. 10.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 3 (book ch. 2) p. 10"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj9", "function_role": "i-chord-color-voicing-over-maj7-symbol", "narrative": "Warnock prescribes Cmaj9 as the preferred voiced realization of a Cmaj7 lead-sheet symbol, establishing the 9th as the default color tone added by the performer. 'To begin, here are four chords that fit over the ii V I progression, with the Cmaj7 and Cmaj9 being two colors of the Cmaj7 sound.' Cmaj9 is the richer of the two and represents real-life jazz comping practice. Chapter 1, p. 4; Chapter 3, p. 11.", "source_principle_ids": ["matt-warnock:beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar:ii-v-i-comping-system"], "source_work_id": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 2 (book ch. 1) p. 4"}, {"source": "beginners-guide-to-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 4 (book ch. 3) p. 11"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj9", "function_role": "i-chord-approach-chord-shape-preservation", "narrative": "When applying approach chords to the Cmaj9 voicing, Warnock prescribes preserving the entire shape and moving it chromatically as a unit -- the voicing is not rearranged for the approach. 'You play a chromatic chord one fret above or below the target chord you're aiming for' using 'the same shape.'
